129.stem: A particle is shot vertically upwards from a point 100 metres above ground level. The position of the particle, $y$ metres above the ground after $t$ seconds, is given by $y(t)=-5t^2+70t+100$.

parts.latex: Find the maximum height above ground level reached by the particle.

Velocity as a rate of change.reason: Only a prerequisite of agreed Particles at rest and changing direction

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: not_when: v=0 for max height belongs to Particles at rest (agreed); nothing beyond velocity used

parts.latex: Find the velocity of the particle, in metres per second, immediately before it hits the ground, leaving your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

Velocity as a rate of change.reason: Velocity as dy/dt of a polynomial displacement is needed for the answer.

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: Displacement is powers of t only with no acceleration: belongs to Velocity as a rate of change.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y(t) &= -5t^2 + 70t + 100 \\ y'(t) &= -10t + 70 \end{aligned}$$
When $y'(t) = 0$,
$$\begin{aligned} -10t + 70 &= 0 \\ t &= 7 \end{aligned}$$
At $t = 7$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -5(7)^2 + 70(7) + 100 \\ &= 345 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the time it takes to reach maximum height, or equivalent merit

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
To find when the particle hits the ground, we solve
$$\begin{aligned} -5t^2 + 70t + 100 &= 0 \\ t^2 - 14t - 20 &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{14 \pm \sqrt{196 + 80}}{2} \\ &= 7 \pm \sqrt{69} \end{aligned}$$
$t = 7 + \sqrt{69}$, since $t > 0$
$$\begin{aligned} y'(7+\sqrt{69}) &= -10(7+\sqrt{69}) + 70 \\ &= -10\sqrt{69} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ a = -10$ and $b = 69$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to solve to find the time $y(t) = 0$, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} f(1.1) &\approx f(1)+0.1\times f'(1) \\ &= 6+0.1\times 2 \\ &= 6.2 \end{aligned}$$
$f'(x)$ is decreasing on this interval ($f'(x)<2$ for $x>1$), so the increase is a little less than $0.2$ and $f(1.1)$ lies in $[6.0,\ 6.2)$.

2319.stem: A ball is thrown upwards from the edge of a cliff and hits the ground below. Its vertical height ($h$) in metres above the ground is given by the formula $h=-t^2+2t+3$ where $t$ is the time in seconds.

figures.cap: solution sketch: velocity graph: straight line from (0,2) through (1,0) to (3,-4)

parts.latex: At what time does the ball hit the ground?
At what time is the ball stationary?
In the box below, graph the velocity function of the ball from the time it is launched until it hits the ground.
Find the total vertical distance travelled by the ball.

solutions.latex:
The ball hits the ground when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+2t+3&=0\\t^2-2t-3&=0\\(t-3)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=3$ or $t=-1$; since $t>0$, $t=3$ seconds.

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
The ball is stationary when its velocity $h'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}h'&=-2t+2\\0&=-2t+2\\t&=1\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
The velocity is $v=h'=-2t+2$, a straight line from $t=0$ to $t=3$ with $v(0)=2$, $v(3)=-4$ and $v=0$ at $t=1$.

\exfigure{292_q24_s1}
criteria: Plots the end points $(0,2)$ and $(3,-4)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, taken as positive: the triangle above the axis ($0\le t\le 1$) and the triangle below it ($1\le t\le 3$).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times 2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 4\\&=1+4\\&=5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards from ground level and lands 8 seconds later in the same place.

Its motion is described by the equation $x = 3t(8-t)$, with displacement $x$ metres and time $t$ seconds. The displacement-time graph is sketched below.

\exfigure{1341_q2_1}

What is the distance travelled by the ball in the first six seconds of motion?

solutions.latex:
The ball reaches its maximum at $t=4$, where $x = 3(4)(4) = 48$.

At $t=6$, $x = 3(6)(2) = 36$.

It rises 48 m, then falls $48-36 = 12$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 48 + (48-36) \\ &= 60 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

meta.source_flag: Source working read 'Distance = 48 + (48 - 12)', which would give 84; the correct value of x at t=6 is 36, so I used 48 - 36 = 12 and the result 60 is unchanged.

parts.latex: A ghost gum tree was planted in 2010. The height of the tree $H$, in metres, is a function of the tree's age, in years, after planting. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of $H'(4)=3.2$?

solutions.latex:
$H'(4)$ is the instantaneous rate of change of height at age 4 years, which is the start of 2014.

So at the start of 2014 the height was increasing at $3.2$ m per year, which matches option C.

parts.latex: Find an equation for the graph in terms of $N$ and $D$ in the form $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$, where $k$ is a constant.
The concert needs an attendance of at least $2000$ in order to make a profit. Find the maximum distance the concert can be from the city centre and still make a profit.
At a point on the graph, the number of people attending is decreasing at the rate of $5$ people per $4$ metres. Find the value of $D$ for this point.

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
The concert makes a profit when $N\ge2000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1\,800\,000}{D}&\ge2000\\ D&\le900\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum distance is } 900 \text{ m}$$

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
Since $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$, differentiating with respect to $D$ gives
$$\dfrac{dN}{dD}=-\dfrac{k}{D^2}$$
The rate is $-\dfrac{5}{4}=-1.25$ people per metre, so
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=\dfrac{-k}{dN/dD}\\ &=\dfrac{-1\,800\,000}{-1.25}\\ &=1\,440\,000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ D=1200 \text{ m}\ (=1.2 \text{ km})$$
criteria: Correct equation for $D^2$, or equivalent merit
